claims.claim: Tracking statistical probabilities might not lead to stream segmentation in the case of quadrisyllabic words in both neonates and adults.
claims.source: We also discovered that tracking statistical probabilities might not lead to stream segmentation in the case of quadrisyllabic words in both neonates and adults, revealing an unsuspected limitation of this mechanism (Benjamin et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Benjamin et al., 2023.

claims.claim: Syllables convey two important pieces of information for humans: what is being said and who is speaking.
claims.source: To test this, we have taken advantage of the fact that syllables convey two important pieces of information for humans: what is being said and who is speaking, that is linguistic content and speaker's identity.
claims.evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about speech perception.

claims.claim: Auditory processing is organised along several hierarchical and parallel pathways integrating different spectro-temporal dimensions.
claims.source: However, as auditory processing is organised along several hierarchical and parallel pathways integrating different spectro-temporal dimensions (Belin et al., 2000; DeWitt and Rauschecker, 2012; Norman-Haignere et al., 2015; Zatorre and Belin, 2001), statistical learning might be computed on one dimension independently of the variation of the other along the linguistic and the voice pathways in parallel.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Belin et al., 2000; DeWitt and Rauschecker, 2012; Norman-Haignere et al., 2015; Zatorre and Belin, 2001.

claims.claim: Phonetic normalisation across speakers has been revealed in infants through behavioural and brain imaging studies.
claims.source: Numerous behavioural and brain imaging studies have revealed phonetic normalisation across speakers in infants (Dehaene-Lambertz and Pena, 2001; Gennari et al., 2021; Kuhl and Miller, 1982).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dehaene-Lambertz and Pena, 2001; Gennari et al., 2021; Kuhl and Miller, 1982.

claims.claim: By the second half of the first year, statistical learning occurs even when different voices are used.
claims.source: By the second half of the first year, statistical learning has also been shown to occur even when different voices are used (Estes and Lew-Williams, 2015) or when natural speech is presented, where syllable production can vary from instance to instance (Hay et al., 2011; Pelucchi et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Estes and Lew-Williams, 2015; Hay et al., 2011; Pelucchi et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Statistical learning occurs when natural speech is presented, where syllable production can vary from instance to instance.
claims.source: By the second half of the first year, statistical learning has also been shown to occur even when different voices are used (Estes and Lew-Williams, 2015) or when natural speech is presented, where syllable production can vary from instance to instance (Hay et al., 2011; Pelucchi et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hay et al., 2011; Pelucchi et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Neonates would compute TPs between syllables even when each syllable is produced by a different speaker.
claims.source: Therefore, we hypothesised that neonates would compute TPs between syllables even when each syllable is produced by a different speaker, relying on a normalisation process at the syllable or phonetic level.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis that is tested in the experiments.

claims.claim: Artificial streams were constructed using six consonant-vowel (CV) syllables produced by six voices, resulting in 36 possible tokens.
claims.source: To study these possibilities, we constructed artificial streams using six consonant-vowel (CV) syllables produced by six voices (Appendix 1—table 1, Appendix 1—table 2), resulting in 36 possible tokens (6 syllables ×6 voices).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design and stimuli used in the study.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1, the structure consisted of the random concatenation of three duplets defined by phonetic content while voices varied randomly.
claims.source: To form the streams, tokens were combined either by imposing structure to their phonetic content (Experiment 1: Structure over Phonemes) or their voice content (Experiment 2: Structure over Voices), while the second dimension varied randomly (Figure 1). The structure consisted of the random concatenation of three duplets (i.e. two-syllable units) defined only by one of the two dimensions.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: In Experiment 2, the structure consisted of the random concatenation of three duplets defined by voice content while phonetic content varied randomly.
claims.source: To form the streams, tokens were combined either by imposing structure to their phonetic content (Experiment 1: Structure over Phonemes) or their voice content (Experiment 2: Structure over Voices), while the second dimension varied randomly (Figure 1). The structure consisted of the random concatenation of three duplets (i.e. two-syllable units) defined only by one of the two dimensions.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Using artificial language with syllables with a fixed duration elicits Steady State Evoked Potentials (SSEP) at the syllable rate.
claims.source: Using artificial language with syllables with a fixed duration elicits Steady State Evoked Potentials (SSEP) at the syllable rate.
claims.evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the neural response to periodic stimuli.

claims.claim: If the artificial language presents a regular structure and if the structure is perceived, then the neural responses reflect the slower frequency of the word as well.
claims.source: Crucially, if the artificial language presents a regular structure (i.e. regular drops in TPs marking word boundaries) and if the structure is perceived, then the neural responses reflect the slower frequency of the word as well (Buiatti et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Buiatti et al., 2009.

claims.claim: The brain activity becomes phase-locked to the regular input, increasing the Inter Trial Coherence (ITC) and power at the input regularity frequencies.
claims.source: In other words, the brain activity becomes phase-locked to the regular input, increasing the Inter Trial Coherence (ITC) and power at the input regularity frequencies.
claims.evidence: This describes the neural mechanism underlying the SSEP response.

claims.claim: 67 participants (34 in Experiment 1 and 33 in Experiment 2) who provided enough data without motion artefacts were included.
claims.source: 67 participants (34 in Experiment 1 and 33 in Experiment 2) who provided enough data without motion artefacts were included (Experiment 1: 19 females; 1–4 days old; mean GA: 39.3 weeks; mean weight: 3387 g; Experiment 2: 15 females; 1–4 days old; mean GA: 39.0 weeks; mean weight: 3363 g).
claims.evidence: This describes the participant sample in the study.

claims.claim: 12 other infants were excluded from the analyses (11 due to fussiness; 1 due to bad data quality).
claims.source: 12 other infants were excluded from the analyses (11 due to fussiness; 1 due to bad data quality).
claims.evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria applied in the study.

claims.claim: Significant entrainment at syllable rate (4 Hz) was observed over a broad set of electrodes in both experiments during Random streams.
claims.source: For the Random streams, we observed significant entrainment at syllable rate (4 Hz) over a broad set of electrodes in both experiments (p<0.05, FDR corrected) and no enhanced activity at the duplet rate for any electrode (p>0.05, FDR corrected).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the neural entrainment analysis presented in the Results section.

claims.claim: No enhanced activity at the duplet rate was observed for any electrode during Random streams.
claims.source: For the Random streams, we observed significant entrainment at syllable rate (4 Hz) over a broad set of electrodes in both experiments (p<0.05, FDR corrected) and no enhanced activity at the duplet rate for any electrode (p>0.05, FDR corrected).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the neural entrainment analysis presented in the Results section.

claims.claim: ITC increased at both the syllable and duplet rate during Structured streams in both experiments.
claims.source: Concerning the Structured streams, ITC increased at both the syllable and duplet rate (p<0.05, FDR corrected) in both experiments (Figure 2A and B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the neural entrainment analysis shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The duplet effect in the Phoneme group was localised over occipital and central-left electrodes.
claims.source: The duplet effect was localised over occipital and central-left electrodes in the Phoneme group and over occipital and temporal-right electrodes in the Voice group.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the neural entrainment analysis describing the topography of the effect.

claims.claim: The duplet effect in the Voice group was localised over occipital and temporal-right electrodes.
claims.source: The duplet effect was localised over occipital and central-left electrodes in the Phoneme group and over occipital and temporal-right electrodes in the Voice group.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the neural entrainment analysis describing the topography of the effect.

claims.claim: Electrodes with significantly higher ITC at the duplet rate during Structured streams than Random streams were found in both experiments.
claims.source: We found electrodes with significantly higher ITC at the duplet rate during Structured streams than Random streams in both experiments (p<0.05, FDR corrected).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the direct comparison of ITC between conditions.

claims.claim: Electrodes with higher entrainment at syllable rate during the Structured than Random streams were found in both experiments.
claims.source: We also found electrodes with higher entrainment at syllable rate during the Structured than Random streams in both experiments (p<0.05, FDR corrected).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the direct comparison of ITC between conditions.

claims.claim: A significant time effect was found in the Phoneme group for ITC at 2 Hz during the long Structured familiarisation.
claims.source: In the Phoneme group, we found a significant time effect (β=4.16 × 10–3, 95% CI=[2.06×10–3, 6.29×10–3], SE = 1.05 × 10–3, p=4 × 10–4)
claims.evidence: This is a result from the Linear Mixed Model analysis of the time course of entrainment.

claims.claim: A significant time effect was found in the Voice group for ITC at 2 Hz during the long Structured familiarisation.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the Linear Mixed Model analysis of the time course of entrainment.

claims.claim: The fixed effect estimating the difference in time effect between the Phoneme and Voice groups was not significant.
claims.source: while the fixed effect estimating the difference between the Phoneme and Voice groups was not significant (β=−1.84 × 10–3, 95% CI=[–6.29×10–3, 2.61×10–3], SE = 2.24 × 10–3, p=0.4).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the Linear Mixed Model comparing the time effects between groups.

claims.claim: The difference between Word and Part-word consisted of a dipole with a median positivity and a left temporal negativity ranging from 400 to 1500ms.
claims.source: The difference between Word and Part-word consisted of a dipole with a median positivity and a left temporal negativity ranging from 400 to 1500ms, with a maximum around 800–900ms (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the ERP analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Cluster-based permutations recovered two significant clusters around 500–1500ms: a frontal-right positive cluster (p=0.019) and a left temporal negative cluster (p=0.0056).
claims.source: Cluster-based permutations recovered two significant clusters around 500–1500ms: a frontal-right positive cluster (p=0.019) and a left temporal negative cluster (p=0.0056).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the cluster-based permutation analysis of ERPs.

claims.claim: A difference between groups was observed consisting of a dipole that started with a right temporal positivity left temporo-occipital negativity around 300ms and rotated anti-clockwise.
claims.source: A difference between groups was observed consisting of a dipole that started with a right temporal positivity left temporo-occipital negativity around 300ms and rotated anti-clockwise to bring the positivity over the frontal electrodes and the negativity at the back of the head (500–800ms; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the ERP analysis comparing groups.

claims.claim: Cluster-based permutations on the Phoneme group vs. Voice group recovered a posterior cluster (p=0.018) around 500ms.
claims.source: Cluster-based permutations on the Phoneme group vs. Voice group recovered a posterior cluster (p=0.018) around 500ms; with no positive cluster reaching significance (p>0.10).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the cluster-based permutation analysis comparing groups.

claims.claim: A cluster-based permutation analysis on the interaction effect showed no significant clusters.
claims.source: A cluster-based permutation analysis on the interaction effect, that is comparing Words - Part-Words between both experiments, showed no significant clusters (p>0.1).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the cluster-based permutation analysis testing for interaction effects.

claims.claim: For the group familiarised with the Phoneme structure, there was a significant difference between the scores attributed to Words and Part-words in adults.
claims.source: For the group familiarised with the Phoneme structure, there was a significant difference between the scores attributed to Words and Part-words (t(26)=2.92, p=0.007, Cohen's d=0.562).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the adult behavioral experiment.

claims.claim: The difference between Words and Part-words was marginally significant for the group familiarised with the Voice structure in adults.
claims.source: The difference was marginally significant for the group familiarised with the Voice structure (t(29)=2.0443, p=0.050, Cohen's d=0.373; Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the adult behavioral experiment shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: A 2-way ANOVA with test-duplets and familiarisation as factors revealed a main effect of Word in adults.
claims.source: A 2-way ANOVA with test-duplets and familiarisation as factors revealed a main effect of Word (F(1,55)=12.52, p=0.0008, ηg2=0.039), no effect of familiarisation (F(1,55) <1), and a significant interaction Word ×Familiarisation (F(1,55) = 5.28, p=0.025, ηg2=0.017).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the adult behavioral experiment.

claims.claim: A 2-way ANOVA with test-duplets and familiarisation as factors revealed a significant interaction Word × Familiarisation in adults.
claims.source: A 2-way ANOVA with test-duplets and familiarisation as factors revealed a main effect of Word (F(1,55)=12.52, p=0.0008, ηg2=0.039), no effect of familiarisation (F(1,55) <1), and a significant interaction Word ×Familiarisation (F(1,55) = 5.28, p=0.025, ηg2=0.017).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the adult behavioral experiment.

claims.claim: Neonates were sensitive to regularities based either on the phonetic or the voice dimensions of speech, even in the presence of a non-informative feature that must be disregarded.
claims.source: We showed that neonates were sensitive to regularities based either on the phonetic or the voice dimensions of speech, even in the presence of a non-informative feature that must be disregarded.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results in both experiments.

claims.claim: Parsing based on statistical information was revealed by steady-state evoked potentials at the duplet rate observed around 2 min after the onset of the familiarisation stream.
claims.source: Parsing based on statistical information was revealed by steady-state evoked potentials at the duplet rate observed around 2 min after the onset of the familiarisation stream and by different ERPs to Words and Part-words presented during a recognition phase in both experiments.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neural entrainment and ERP results.

claims.claim: Statistical learning was possible despite variations in the other dimension, showing that this mechanism operates at a stage when these dimensions have already been separated along different processing pathways.
claims.source: Despite variations in the other dimension, statistical learning was possible, showing that this mechanism operates at a stage when these dimensions have already been separated along different processing pathways.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claims.claim: Linguistic content and voice identity are calculated independently and in parallel.
claims.source: Our results, thus, revealed that linguistic content and voice identity are calculated independently and in parallel.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing successful learning in both experiments.

claims.claim: Even in newborns, the syllable is not a holistic unit.
claims.source: This result confirms that, even in newborns, the syllable is not a holistic unit (Gennari et al., 2021)
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the current results and a citation to Gennari et al., 2021.

claims.claim: The rich temporo-frequential spectrum of speech is processed in parallel along different networks, probably using different integration factors.
claims.source: but that the rich temporo-frequential spectrum of speech is processed in parallel along different networks, probably using different integration factors (Boemio et al., 2005; Moerel et al., 2012; Zatorre and Belin, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion supported by citations to Boemio et al., 2005; Moerel et al., 2012; Zatorre and Belin, 2001.

claims.claim: Even sleeping neonates distinctly applied statistical learning to potentially all dimensions in which speech is factorised in the auditory cortex.
claims.source: While statistical learning has already been described in many domains in neonates and young infants (Fló et al., 2019; Fló et al., 2022b; Kirkham et al., 2002; Kudo et al., 2011), we add here that even sleeping neonates distinctly applied it to potentially all dimensions in which speech is factorised in the auditory cortex (Gennari et al., 2021; Gwilliams et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The results contribute to a growing body of evidence supporting the universality of statistical learning.
claims.source: Our result contribute to a growing body of evidence supporting the universality of statistical learning —albeit with potential quantitative differences (Frost et al., 2015; Ren and Wang, 2023; Santolin and Saffran, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion supported by citations to Frost et al., 2015; Ren and Wang, 2023; Santolin and Saffran, 2018.

claims.claim: Statistical learning might be rooted in associative learning processes relying on the co-existence of event representations driven by slow activation decays.
claims.source: This mechanism might be rooted in associative learning processes relying on the co-existence of event representations driven by slow activation decays (Benjamin et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation to Benjamin et al., 2024.

claims.claim: No clear processing advantage for the linguistic dimension over the voice dimension was observed in neonates.
claims.source: We observed no clear processing advantage for the linguistic dimension over the voice dimension in neonates.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claims.claim: The ability to track regularities in parallel for different speech features provides newborns with a powerful tool to create associations between recurring events and uncover structure.
claims.source: The ability to track regularities in parallel for different speech features provides newborns with a powerful tool to create associations between recurring events and uncover structure.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claims.claim: The word-rate steady-state response (2 Hz) for the group of infants exposed to structure over phonemes was over posterior electrodes and left lateralised over central electrodes.
claims.source: The word-rate steady-state response (2 Hz) for the group of infants exposed to structure over phonemes was over posterior electrodes and left lateralised over central electrodes, while the group of infants hearing structure over voices showed mostly entrainment over posterior and right temporal electrodes.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the neural entrainment analysis describing topographical differences.

claims.claim: The group of infants hearing structure over voices showed mostly entrainment over posterior and right temporal electrodes.
claims.source: The word-rate steady-state response (2 Hz) for the group of infants exposed to structure over phonemes was over posterior electrodes and left lateralised over central electrodes, while the group of infants hearing structure over voices showed mostly entrainment over posterior and right temporal electrodes.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the neural entrainment analysis describing topographical differences.

claims.claim: Recent brain imaging studies in infants show hemispheric biases in precursors of later networks.
claims.source: Recent brain imaging studies in infants do indeed show hemispheric biases in precursors of later networks (Blasi et al., 2011; Dehaene-Lambertz et al., 2010; Mahmoudzadeh et al., 2013), even if specialisation increases during development (Shultz et al., 2014; Sylvester et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blasi et al., 2011; Dehaene-Lambertz et al., 2010; Mahmoudzadeh et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Specialisation increases during development.
claims.source: Recent brain imaging studies in infants do indeed show hemispheric biases in precursors of later networks (Blasi et al., 2011; Dehaene-Lambertz et al., 2010; Mahmoudzadeh et al., 2013), even if specialisation increases during development (Shultz et al., 2014; Sylvester et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Shultz et al., 2014; Sylvester et al., 2023.

claims.claim: A dipole, consisting of a posterior negative pole and a frontal positivity, was recorded around 500ms following linguistic duplets but not voice duplets.
claims.source: In the test phase using isolated duplets, we observed a significant difference between groups: A dipole, consisting of a posterior negative pole and a frontal positivity, was recorded around 500ms following linguistic duplets but not voice duplets.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the ERP analysis comparing groups.

claims.claim: The component observed around 500ms might be a precursor of the N400.
claims.source: Given its topography, latency and the phonetic context in which it appears, this component might be a precursor of the N400, a negative deflection at 200–600ms over central-parietal electrodes elicited by lexico-semantic manipulations in adults (Kutas and Federmeier, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the topography and latency of the component, supported by a citation to Kutas and Federmeier, 2011.

claims.claim: The N400 is a negative deflection at 200–600ms over central-parietal electrodes elicited by lexico-semantic manipulations in adults.
claims.source: Given its topography, latency and the phonetic context in which it appears, this component might be a precursor of the N400, a negative deflection at 200–600ms over central-parietal electrodes elicited by lexico-semantic manipulations in adults (Kutas and Federmeier, 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kutas and Federmeier, 2011.

claims.claim: A posterior negativity has been reported in infants as young as five months when hearing their own name compared to a stranger's name.
claims.source: For example, a posterior negativity has been reported in infants as young as five months when hearing their own name compared to a stranger's name (Parise et al., 2010)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Parise et al., 2010.

claims.claim: A posterior negativity has been reported in infants when a pseudo-word was consistently vs inconsistently associated with an object.
claims.source: when a pseudo-word was consistently vs inconsistently associated with an object (Friedrich and Friederici, 2011)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Friedrich and Friederici, 2011.

claims.claim: A posterior negativity has been reported in infants when they saw unexpected vs expected actions.
claims.source: and when they saw unexpected vs expected actions (Reid et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reid et al., 2009.

claims.claim: An N400 has been reported in adults listening to an artificial language after prior exposure to isolated pseudo-words.
claims.source: For instance, Sanders et al., 2002 observed an N400 in adults listening to an artificial language after prior exposure to isolated pseudo-words.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sanders et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Larger N400 amplitudes have been demonstrated in adults when listening to structured streams compared to random sequences of syllables.
claims.source: Other studies have demonstrated larger N400 amplitudes in adults when listening to structured streams compared to random sequences, whether these sequences consisted of syllables (Cunillera et al., 2006; Cunillera et al., 2009), tones (Abla et al., 2008), or shapes (Abla and Okanoya, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cunillera et al., 2006; Cunillera et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Larger N400 amplitudes have been demonstrated in adults when listening to structured streams compared to random sequences of tones.
claims.source: Other studies have demonstrated larger N400 amplitudes in adults when listening to structured streams compared to random sequences, whether these sequences consisted of syllables (Cunillera et al., 2006; Cunillera et al., 2009), tones (Abla et al., 2008), or shapes (Abla and Okanoya, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Abla et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Larger N400 amplitudes have been demonstrated in adults when listening to structured streams compared to random sequences of shapes.
claims.source: Other studies have demonstrated larger N400 amplitudes in adults when listening to structured streams compared to random sequences, whether these sequences consisted of syllables (Cunillera et al., 2006; Cunillera et al., 2009), tones (Abla et al., 2008), or shapes (Abla and Okanoya, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Abla and Okanoya, 2009.

claims.claim: Phonetic regularities, but not voice regularities, would induce a lexical search during the presentation of the isolated duplets or at least activate a proto-lexical network.
claims.source: However, some inferences can still be drawn regarding the differences between the phoneme and voice experiments. Neural responses in both the learning and recognition phases could reflect a top-down effect: Phonetic regularities, but not voice regularities, would induce a lexical search during the presentation of the isolated duplets or at least activate a proto-lexical network.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed differences between experiments.

claims.claim: Infants extract and store possible word forms even before associating them with a clear meaning.
claims.source: Previous evidence suggests that infants extract and store possible word forms even before associating them with a clear meaning (Jusczyk and Hohne, 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jusczyk and Hohne, 1997.

claims.claim: Stronger fMRI activation for forward speech than backward speech in the left angular gyrus in 3-month-old infants has been linked to the activations of possible word forms in a proto-lexicon for native language sentences.
claims.source: For example, stronger fMRI activation for forward speech than backward speech in the left angular gyrus in 3-month-old infants has been linked to the activations of possible word forms in a proto-lexicon for native language sentences (Dehaene-Lambertz et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dehaene-Lambertz et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Chunks extracted from the speech stream serve as candidate words to which meanings can be attached.
claims.source: Similarly, Shukla et al., 2011 demonstrated that chunks extracted from the speech stream serve as candidate words to which meanings can be attached.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shukla et al., 2011.

claims.claim: 6-month-olds spontaneously associated a pseudo-word extracted from natural sentences with a visual object.
claims.source: In their study, 6-month-olds spontaneously associated a pseudo-word extracted from natural sentences with a visual object.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the citation to Shukla et al., 2011 in the preceding sentence.

claims.claim: Only speech chunks based on phonetic regularities, and not voice regularities, are viable word candidates.
claims.source: Although their experiment relied on TP and prosodic cues to extract the word, while our study only used statistical cues, this spontaneous bias to treat possible word forms as referring to a meaning (see also Bergelson and Aslin, 2017) might trigger activation along a lexicon pathway, explaining the difference between the two experiments: Only speech chunks based on phonetic regularities, and not voice regularities, are viable word candidates.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed differences between experiments and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Adults demonstrated some learning of voice duplets despite several years of exposure to speech.
claims.source: Finally, we would like to emphasise that it is highly unnatural for a word not to be produced by the same speaker, nor for speakers to exhibit the kind of statistical relationships used here. Despite several years of exposure to speech, adults still demonstrated some learning of voice duplets, supporting the hypothesis of a general and automatic statistical learning ability.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the adult behavioral results.

claims.claim: Adults clearly displayed an advantage for phonetic regularities over voice regularities, revealed by the significant interaction Familiarisation × Word.
claims.source: However, they also clearly displayed an advantage for phonetic regularities over voice regularities, revealed by the significant interaction Familiarisation ×Word, not observed in neonates.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the adult behavioral results.

claims.claim: Statistical learning is a general learning mechanism, probably operating on common computational principles across neural networks but within different neural networks with a different chain of operations.
claims.source: Altogether, our results show that statistical learning works similarly on different speech features in human neonates with no clear advantage for computing linguistically relevant regularities in speech. This supports the idea that statistical learning is a general learning mechanism, probably operating on common computational principles across neural networks (Benjamin et al., 2024) but within different neural networks with a different chain of operations
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and supported by a citation to Benjamin et al., 2024.

claims.claim: Phonetic regularities induce a supplementary component not seen in the case of voice regularities that is related to a lexical N400.
claims.source: phonetic regularities induce a supplementary component –not seen in the case of voice regularities—that we related to a lexical N400.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ERP results showing differences between experiments.

claims.claim: Participants were healthy-full-term neonates with normal pregnancy and birth (GA >38 weeks, Apgar scores ≥7/8 at 1/5 min, birthweight >2.5 Kg, cranial perimeter ≥33.0 cm).
claims.source: Participants were healthy-full-term neonates with normal pregnancy and birth (GA >38 weeks, Apgar scores ≥7/8 at 1/5 min, birthweight >2.5 Kg, cranial perimeter ≥33.0 cm), tested at the Port Royal Maternity (AP-HP), in Paris, France.
claims.evidence: This describes the participant inclusion criteria.

claims.evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claims.claim: The stimuli were synthesised using the MBROLA diphone database.

claims.evidence: This describes the method used to create the stimuli, supported by a citation to Dutoit et al., 1996.

claims.source: Syllables had a consonant-vowel structure and lasted 250ms (consonants 90ms, vowels 160ms).
claims.evidence: This describes the properties of the stimuli used in the study.

claims.claim: Six different syllables (ki, da, pe, tu, bo, gɛ) and six different voices were used.
claims.source: Six different syllables (ki, da, pe, tu, bo, gɛ) and six different voices were used (fr3, fr1, fr7, fr2, it4, fr4), resulting in a total of 36 syllable-voice combinations, from now on, tokens.
claims.evidence: This describes the stimuli used in the study.

claims.claim: The learning stream lasted 120 s, with each duplet appearing 80 times.

results.result: Neonates can compute transitional probabilities (TPs) on one speech dimension (phonemes or voices) despite irrelevant variation on the other dimension. This was demonstrated through neural entrainment at both syllable (4 Hz) and duplet (2 Hz) rates during structured streams in both experiments, and distinct ERPs to Words versus Part-words during recognition testing.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5, C37-C39, C42-C43, and C56-C59 collectively provide converging evidence from neural entrainment (ITC analysis) and ERP measures showing that neonates successfully learned statistical regularities in both the phoneme and voice dimensions. The experimental design appropriately controlled for acoustic confounds by using identical tokens across conditions, and statistical tests with FDR correction support the findings.

results.result: Neural entrainment at the duplet rate (2 Hz) increased significantly over time during structured familiarization in both the Phoneme group (β=4.16×10⁻³, p=4×10⁻⁴) and Voice group (β=2.46×10⁻³, p=0.03), with no significant difference in the time effect between groups (p=0.4).
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C46 report results from Linear Mixed Model analyses showing learning time courses. The statistical approach is appropriate for longitudinal data with random effects for subjects. The lack of significant difference between groups (C46) supports the conclusion that learning occurs similarly for both dimensions, though the steeper slope in the Phoneme group suggests possible quantitative differences.

results.result: The topography of neural entrainment at the duplet rate differed between experiments: the Phoneme group showed entrainment over occipital and central-left electrodes, while the Voice group showed entrainment over occipital and temporal-right electrodes.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C41 and C67-C68 describe topographical differences suggesting distinct neural networks for processing phoneme versus voice regularities. However, the authors acknowledge that group comparisons did not survive multiple comparison corrections, and the between-subjects design limits statistical power for detecting interaction effects. The topographical differences are suggestive but require within-subject replication.

results.result: ERPs to Words versus Part-words showed a dipole with median positivity and left temporal negativity (400-1500ms). A significant difference between groups was observed around 500ms, with a posterior negative component appearing only for linguistic duplets (Phoneme group) but not voice duplets (Voice group).
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C51 and C71 report ERP results from cluster-based permutation analyses showing both main effects of test-duplet type and familiarization type. The statistical approach is appropriate for ERP data, and the lack of significant interaction (C51) is appropriately reported. The finding that only phoneme regularities elicited the posterior negativity is well-supported by the data.

results.result: The posterior negative ERP component observed around 500ms following linguistic duplets (but not voice duplets) is interpreted as a potential N400 precursor, suggesting activation of a proto-lexical network triggered by phonetic regularities.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C72, and C90 propose that the observed component is an N400 precursor based on topography and latency. While the interpretation is plausible and supported by citations to prior infant N400 literature (C73-C80), this remains speculative. The component's functional significance as reflecting lexical processing versus other cognitive processes cannot be definitively established from the current data alone.

results.result: Adult participants showed significant learning for phoneme regularities (p=0.007) and marginally significant learning for voice regularities (p=0.050), with a significant interaction (p=0.025) indicating an advantage for phonetic over voice regularities not observed in neonates.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C55 and C87-C88 report adult behavioral results with appropriate statistical tests (t-tests and 2-way ANOVA). The marginal significance for voice learning (p=0.050) is at the threshold but appropriately reported. The significant interaction demonstrates a developmental difference between neonates and adults, though the authors acknowledge this could reflect explicit versus implicit task demands or other factors.

results.result: Statistical learning operates as a general mechanism across different speech dimensions (phonemes and voices) in neonates, supporting the universality of statistical learning. The mechanism likely operates on common computational principles but within different neural networks with distinct processing pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 and C89 present the main theoretical conclusions supported by the experimental findings and extensive citations to prior literature. The conclusion that statistical learning is general is well-supported by the successful learning in both experiments. However, the claim about 'common computational principles' (C89) is more speculative and relies heavily on cited theoretical work (Benjamin et al., 2024).

results.result: No clear processing advantage for the linguistic dimension over the voice dimension was observed in neonates, suggesting that the ability to track regularities in parallel for different speech features provides a powerful learning tool from birth.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 are supported by the lack of significant interaction effects in the neonate data (C46, C51) and comparable learning in both experiments. This contrasts with the adult data showing an advantage for phoneme regularities (C88), highlighting a developmental difference. The conclusion is appropriately qualified as 'no clear advantage' given the suggestive but non-significant topographical differences.

results.result: Phonetic regularities, but not voice regularities, may induce activation of a proto-lexical network during duplet presentation, as only speech chunks based on phonetic regularities are viable word candidates.
results.evaluation: Claims C81 and C86 present speculative interpretations of the ERP differences between experiments. While supported by citations to prior work on proto-lexical processing (C82-C85), this interpretation goes beyond what the current data can definitively establish. Alternative explanations for the ERP differences are not fully ruled out, and the proto-lexical interpretation requires additional experimental validation.

results.result: The study used appropriate methods including synthesized speech stimuli with controlled transitional probabilities, 128-electrode EEG recording in sleeping neonates, and rigorous preprocessing pipelines. Sample sizes were 34 neonates (Experiment 1), 33 neonates (Experiment 2), and 57 adults, with appropriate exclusion criteria and ethical approvals.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C31 and C35-C36, C91-C102 describe methodological details that are clearly documented and appropriate for the research questions. The experimental design cleverly uses identical acoustic tokens across conditions to control for acoustic confounds. Sample sizes are reasonable for infant EEG studies, though larger samples would increase power for detecting interaction effects. The preprocessing pipeline (APICE) is validated in prior work.

results.result: The introduction establishes prior work on statistical learning, including the seminal Saffran et al. (1996) study showing 8-month-olds can extract words using transitional probabilities, and subsequent demonstrations of statistical learning across domains, species, and in neonates.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C8-C27 accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. These background claims establish the context for the current study and are well-supported by the cited references. The characterization of statistical learning as a general mechanism across domains and species (C2, C20) is consistent with review literature.

results.result: The authors hypothesized that neonates would compute TPs between syllables even when each syllable is produced by a different speaker, relying on phonetic normalization.
results.evaluation: Claim C28 states the primary hypothesis tested in Experiment 1, which is clearly supported by the experimental results (C3-C5, C56-C57). This hypothesis is well-motivated by prior work on phonetic normalization in infants (C25-C27).

results.result: The study leverages established knowledge that periodic syllable presentation elicits steady-state evoked potentials (SSEP) at the syllable rate, and that perceived structure in the stream produces neural entrainment at the word rate through phase-locking.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 describe the theoretical basis for using neural entrainment as a measure of statistical learning. This is well-established methodology supported by prior work (C33 cites Buiatti et al., 2009) and appropriately applied in the current study.

results.result: Prior brain imaging studies show hemispheric biases in precursors of later networks in infants, though specialization increases during development.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 accurately cite prior literature on hemispheric specialization in infant brain development. These claims provide context for interpreting the topographical differences observed between experiments, though the authors appropriately caution about over-interpreting these differences.

results.result: Prior literature documents N400 components in adults and N400-like posterior negativities in infants in various semantic and statistical learning contexts, as well as evidence that infants extract and store possible word forms before associating them with meanings.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C80 and C82-C85 accurately summarize prior literature on N400 components and proto-lexical processing with appropriate citations. These claims provide the theoretical foundation for interpreting the posterior negativity observed in the current study as a potential N400 precursor.

results.result: The results suggest that multiple input regularities can be processed in parallel from birth, and statistical learning might be rooted in associative learning processes relying on slow activation decays.
results.evaluation: Claim C7 is a well-supported conclusion from the experimental results showing successful learning in both experiments. Claim C64 is more speculative, presenting a mechanistic hypothesis supported by citation to Benjamin et al. (2024) but not directly tested in the current study.

results.result: Neonates demonstrated neural entrainment at both syllable (4 Hz) and duplet (2 Hz) rates during structured streams in both phoneme and voice experiments, with no entrainment at duplet rate during random streams. This indicates that neonates can compute transitional probabilities on one dimension (phonemes or voices) despite irrelevant variation on the other dimension.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirmed these findings. Reviewer 1 stated 'the study reveals that newborns compute TPs over linguistic and non-linguistic features of speech, these are calculated independently.' Reviewer 2 noted 'the authors found evidence for both, stronger entrainment to regularities' and called the paper 'very convincing.' Reviewer 3 confirmed 'newborns showed neural entrainment to the regularities implemented in the stream' in both experiments.

results.result: Event-related potential (ERP) analysis revealed distinct responses to Words versus Part-words in both experiments, with a dipole pattern showing median positivity and left temporal negativity (400-1500ms). Cluster-based permutations identified significant frontal-right positive and left temporal negative clusters, though the interaction effect between experiments was not significant.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these ERP findings without challenge. Reviewer 1 noted 'Newborns showed also different neural activity in response to the words and part words.' Reviewer 2 stated the authors 'found evidence for...ERP differences in response to violations of previously introduced regularities.' The lack of significant interaction was not questioned by any reviewer.

results.result: Only linguistic duplets (phoneme-based) elicited a specific ERP component around 500ms consisting of a posterior negative pole and frontal positivity, which the authors interpret as a potential N400 precursor suggesting early lexical processing. This component was not observed for voice duplets.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly endorsed this key finding. Reviewer 2 stated 'violations of phoneme regularities elicited an ERP pattern which the authors argue might index a precursor of the N400 response.' Reviewer 3 noted 'only the duplets defined by transitional probabilities over syllables (aka word forms) elicited a N400 ERP component.' The interpretation as a potential N400 precursor was accepted by all reviewers without objection.

results.result: The topography of neural entrainment at the duplet rate differed between experiments: phoneme-based structure showed left-lateralized central and occipital activation, while voice-based structure showed right temporal and occipital activation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these topographical differences without challenge. Reviewer 2 praised 'the combination of neural entrainment and ERP analysis' and found the paper 'very convincing.' The differential lateralization patterns were not questioned and align with the reviewers' acceptance of independent parallel processing pathways.

results.result: The results demonstrate that multiple input regularities (phonetic and voice) can be processed in parallel from birth along different processing pathways, indicating that speech is not processed as a holistic unit but is factorized into different dimensions that are computed independently.
results.evaluation: This central conclusion was strongly endorsed by all reviewers. Reviewer 1 stated 'the study reveals that newborns compute TPs over linguistic and non-linguistic features of speech, these are calculated independently.' The editor noted the manuscript 'showing that statistical learning in neonates occurs robustly and is not limited to linguistic features but occurs across different domains.' Reviewer 3 confirmed 'statistical learning operates in parallel and independently on different dimensions of the speech already at birth.'

results.result: No clear processing advantage for the linguistic dimension over the voice dimension was observed in neonates, though adults showed a significant advantage for phonetic regularities (revealed by the interaction Familiarisation × Word).
results.evaluation: Reviewers expressed some reservation about this conclusion. Reviewer 1 noted as a weakness: 'in order to fully conclude that there is no obvious advantage for the linguistic dimension in neonates, future studies should pit both dimensions against each other, to determine whether statistical learning weighs linguistic and non-linguistic features equally.' This suggests the current design does not definitively establish equal processing, though reviewers did not reject the claim outright.

results.result: Adult behavioral experiments showed significant learning of phoneme-based duplets and marginally significant learning of voice-based duplets, with a significant interaction indicating an advantage for phonetic regularities. Adults demonstrated some learning of voice duplets despite the unnaturalness of the task.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the adult control data without objection. Reviewer 3 noted 'There is also a behavioral experiment with adults that acts like a control study for newborns' and appreciated this methodological addition. The adult results were treated as supporting evidence for the general statistical learning mechanism while showing developmental differences.

results.result: The study employed a well-designed experimental paradigm using artificial speech streams with 36 tokens (6 syllables × 6 voices), structured either by phoneme or voice regularities. 67 neonates were tested with EEG (34 in Experiment 1, 33 in Experiment 2), with 12 excluded, and 57 adults were tested online.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praised the methodological approach. Reviewer 1 stated 'the study combines a highly replicated and well-established paradigm...with a state-of-the-art EEG analysis' and noted 'The sample size of the groups is sufficient to ensure power, and the design and analysis are solid.' Reviewer 2 called it 'a clever manipulation' and noted 'implementing this paradigm in a comparably large sample of neonates is impressive.' Reviewer 3 stated 'The design is robust and appropriate for EEG with newborns.'

results.result: The findings contribute to evidence supporting the universality of statistical learning as a general learning mechanism, potentially rooted in associative learning processes, providing newborns with a powerful tool to create associations and uncover structure.
results.evaluation: Reviewers endorsed these broader implications. Reviewer 1 stated the research 'furthers our knowledge of the scope of the statistical learning mechanism, which is confirmed to be a general-purpose powerful tool.' The editor noted the findings are 'highly relevant for researchers working in several domains.' Reviewer 3 stated the results 'add new information about how statistical learning works at the beginning of postnatal life.'

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive background on statistical learning, including prior findings in infants, adults, and non-human animals across domains, as well as theoretical context about auditory processing pathways, phonetic normalization, and N400 components in development.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge any of the background claims or theoretical framing. Reviewer 3 specifically noted 'I appreciated the clarity of the Methods section' and 'I appreciated how the authors addressed my previous comments and concerns...the adjustment to the theoretical framework suits well.' The extensive citations and background knowledge were implicitly accepted through the reviewers' overall positive assessments.

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support the core findings of neural entrainment and statistical learning in neonates (C3-C5, C37-C39, C42-C43, C56-C57). OpenEval includes additional claims about time course analysis (C44-C46) not explicitly mentioned in peer review. Both evaluations affirm successful learning in both phoneme and voice dimensions with appropriate experimental controls.

OpenEval evaluates Linear Mixed Model time course results (C44-C46) as SUPPORTED, noting appropriate statistical methods and lack of significant group differences. Peer reviewers implicitly accepted these findings as part of their overall endorsement of the entrainment results, though they did not explicitly discuss the time course analysis separately.

Perfect claim overlap (C40-C41, C67-C68) but different evaluations. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to lack of statistical significance after multiple comparison correction and between-subjects design limitations. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting topographical differences without challenge and praising the combination of neural entrainment and ERP analysis.

Strong agreement on ERP findings (C47-C51). Both evaluations support the cluster-based permutation results showing main effects and lack of interaction. OpenEval explicitly notes the appropriateness of the statistical approach, while peer reviewers accepted findings without objection and found the evidence 'very convincing.'

Both address N400 precursor interpretation (C6, C72, C90). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting the interpretation is plausible but speculative and cannot be definitively established. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, explicitly endorsing the N400 precursor interpretation without expressing reservations about its speculative nature.

Strong agreement on adult behavioral results (C52-C55, C87). Both evaluations support the findings with appropriate statistical tests. OpenEval notes the marginal significance for voice learning (p=0.050) and acknowledges alternative explanations for developmental differences. Peer reviewers accepted the adult control data as supporting evidence without objection.

Both address main theoretical conclusions about general statistical learning (C60-C62, C89). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED for the general learning conclusion but notes the 'common computational principles' claim (C89) is more speculative. Peer reviewers strongly endorsed these conclusions, with all three reviewers explicitly affirming the general-purpose nature of statistical learning.

Both address the claim of no clear advantage for linguistic dimension in neonates (C65-C66). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED based on lack of significant interactions, appropriately qualified as 'no clear advantage.' Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 1 noting that future within-subject studies are needed to definitively establish equal processing.

OpenEval evaluates proto-lexical processing interpretation (C81, C86) as UNCERTAIN, noting it is speculative and requires additional validation. Peer reviewers implicitly accepted this theoretical framing as part of their overall positive assessment, with Reviewer 3 specifically praising the theoretical framework adjustments.

Perfect claim overlap on methodological details (C29-C31, C35-C36, C91-C102). Both strongly support the experimental design and methods. OpenEval notes appropriate controls and validated preprocessing pipeline while acknowledging sample size limitations for interaction effects. Peer reviewers praised the 'state-of-the-art' approach, 'clever manipulation,' and 'robust design.'

Both address background literature and theoretical context (C1-C2, C8-C27). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting accurate summarization with appropriate citations. Peer reviewers implicitly accepted all background claims through their overall positive assessments, with no challenges to the theoretical framing or literature review.

OpenEval evaluates the primary hypothesis (C28) as SUPPORTED based on experimental results. Peer reviewers did not separately evaluate this hypothesis statement but implicitly accepted it through their endorsement of the overall study design and findings.

OpenEval evaluates the neural entrainment methodology rationale (C32-C34) as SUPPORTED, noting well-established methods. Peer reviewers implicitly accepted this methodological approach through their praise of the 'well-established paradigm' and 'state-of-the-art EEG analysis.'

OpenEval evaluates hemispheric specialization literature citations (C69-C70) as SUPPORTED, noting they provide appropriate context. Peer reviewers did not separately evaluate these background claims but accepted them as part of the overall theoretical framework.

OpenEval evaluates N400 and proto-lexical processing literature (C73-C80, C82-C85) as SUPPORTED, noting accurate citations providing theoretical foundation. Peer reviewers implicitly accepted this literature review through their endorsement of the N400 precursor interpretation and overall theoretical framework.

OpenEval evaluates the general statistical learning conclusion (C7) as SUPPORTED and the mechanistic hypothesis (C64) as more speculative. Peer reviewers strongly endorsed the general learning conclusion (C7) as central to the paper's contribution, with explicit affirmation from all reviewers.

Both address broader implications (C64, C66). OpenEval notes C64 is speculative and not directly tested. Peer reviewers endorsed the broader implications about general-purpose learning mechanisms, viewing the findings as 'highly relevant for researchers working in several domains.'

Minor overlap on C71 (posterior negativity for phoneme regularities). OpenEval includes this in broader ERP analysis evaluation (SUPPORTED), while peer reviewers include it in their endorsement of the N400 precursor interpretation (SUPPORTED).
